equation_request.abstract: The Quantum Fourier Transform offers an interesting way to perform arithmetic operations on a quantum computer. We review existing Quantum Fourier Transform adders and multipliers and comment some simple variations that extend their capabilities. These modified circuits can perform modular and non-modular arithmetic operations and work with signed integers. Among the operations, we discuss a quantum method to compute the weighted average of a series of inputs in the transform domain. One of the circuits, the controlled weighted sum, can be interpreted as a circuit to compute the inner product of two data vectors.

specification.problem: Perform arithmetic (addition, weighted sum / inner product) on a quantum computer in the Fourier (transform) domain using QFT-based adders and multipliers, with modular/non-modular and signed-integer variants.
specification.reconstruction_scope: Smallest useful construction: a Draper-style QFT adder (modular addition of a classical constant or register) and its extension to a weighted sum accumulating sum_j w_j x_j in the phase domain, with a tiny instance of n=3 target qubits and two inputs. Outside scope: the paper's specific circuit variants, signed-integer handling details, controlled versions, the weighted-average method (including any division/normalization), and resource counts.

symbols.meaning: number of qubits in the accumulator register
quantum Fourier transform on n qubits

equations.label: QFT definition
equations.description: QFT of a computational basis state, defining the transform domain.
equations.justification: Standard definition; the abstract only names the QFT.

equations.label: Phase-domain addition
equations.description: Adding a in the Fourier domain via phase rotations gives a+b modulo N; exact equality in the modular sense.
equations.justification: Draper adder background; the abstract mentions QFT adders but gives no formulas.
assumptions: Phases applied as single-qubit (controlled) rotations by 2\pi a/2^{l}

equations.label: Full adder circuit
assumptions: Non-modular result requires an extra carry qubit, i.e. n larger than bit length of a+b

equations.label: Weighted sum accumulation
equations.latex: |0\rangle_{\phi}\mapsto|\phi(S \bmod N)\rangle,\quad S=\sum_j w_jx_j,\quad \text{phase }\exp\!\Big(\tfrac{2\pi i k}{N}\sum_j w_jx_j\Big)
equations.description: Controlled phase rotations by bits of x_j scaled by w_j accumulate the weighted sum in the accumulator, modulo N. This is the inner product of vectors w and x.
equations.abstract_quote: One of the circuits, the controlled weighted sum, can be interpreted as a circuit to compute the inner product of two data vectors.
equations.justification: The inner-product interpretation implies accumulating sum_j w_j x_j; the specific phase implementation is the standard multiplier construction, not confirmed by the abstract.
assumptions: N large enough to avoid wraparound if exact S is desired

registers.name: acc
registers.role: accumulator held in Fourier basis, holds result modulo 2^n

registers.name: x
registers.size: m per input (instance: 2 inputs, 2 qubits each)

specification.initial_state: acc in |0>^n (then QFT applied), x registers in computational basis encoding of x_j, big-endian assumed, unsigned integers

steps.description: For each input j and each bit of x_j, apply controlled phase rotations on acc scaled by w_j 2^l to accumulate the weighted sum in the phase domain.
Apply inverse QFT to acc to return to the computational basis, holding S mod N.

specification.measurement: Measure acc in the computational basis to read S mod 2^n.
specification.classical_postprocessing: Interpret outcome as an integer; two's-complement reinterpretation would be needed for signed results (not specified by the abstract). Any weighted average would require separate division by the sum of weights, not an exact result from this circuit.
assumptions: No scope was provided; chose Draper-style adder plus weighted-sum accumulation as the smallest construction.
Instance: n=3, two 2-bit inputs, small integer weights.
Details of the paper's variants were not available from the abstract.
